Cat FAQ

Everything you wanted to know about our feline friends.

Select a question to reveal the answer.

  • Cats purr by rapidly dilating and constricting the glottis — the part of the larynx surrounding the vocal cords — during both inhalation and exhalation, producing a continuous vibration at 25–150 Hz.

    While purring is most associated with contentment, cats also purr when anxious, injured, or giving birth. Some researchers believe the frequency range may even promote bone healing and muscle repair, making purring a built-in self-soothing mechanism.

  • Kneading — also called "making biscuits" — is a behaviour retained from kittenhood, when nursing kittens press against their mother's belly to stimulate milk flow.

    Adult cats knead soft surfaces (and their favourite humans) as a sign of comfort and contentment. Cats also have scent glands in their paw pads, so kneading doubles as a way to mark a cherished spot as their own.

  • Cats are obligate carnivores with strong predatory instincts. When a cat drops a prey item at your feet — whether a mouse, bird, or toy — it is sharing a successful hunt with a member of its social group, much as a mother cat would bring prey back to teach her kittens.

    Spayed females are especially prone to this behaviour because the drive to hunt remains even when reproduction doesn't. Consider it a compliment: your cat sees you as family worth feeding.

I should add an h2 before the list or restructure the headings so they flow properly from h1 to h2 to h3.
